Motion for Summary Judgment, or in the alternative, Motion for Summary Adjudication

Moving Party: Defendant Brenda Dietlein

Responding Party: Plaintiffs Robert Farias, individually and dba Farias Jett & Company, and Lakeshore Investment, LLC

 

T/R:     DEFENDANT’S MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT, OR IN THE ALTERNATIVE, MOTION FOR SUMMARY ADJUDICATION IS DENIED.

 

DEFENDANT TO NOTICE.

 

If the parties wish to submit on the tentative, please email the courtroom at SMCdept54@lacourt.org with notice to opposing counsel (or self-represented party) before 8:00 am on the day of the hearing

 

The Court considers the moving papers, opposition, and reply.

 

BACKGROUND

 

On February 2, 2022, Plaintiffs Robert Farias, individually and dba Farias Jett & Company, and Lakeshore Investment, LLC filed the operative first amended complaint against Defendants Brenda Dietlein and Glendale Centre Theatre, asserting causes of action for (1) breach of contract; (2) account stated; (3) money had and received; and (4) unjust enrichment. Plaintiffs allege Defendant Dietlein hired them to perform accounting services in connection with Dietlein’s marriage dissolution. Plaintiffs allege they performed the services and Defendants have failed to pay $200,000.00 in accounting fees. Plaintiffs also allege they loaned Defendants money, which has yet to be repaid.

 

ANALYSIS

 

“The purpose of the law of summary judgment is to provide courts with a mechanism to cut through the parties' pleadings in order to determine whether, despite their allegations, trial is in fact necessary to resolve their dispute.” (Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 826, 843.) Trial judges are required “to grant summary judgment if all the evidence submitted, and ‘all inferences reasonably deducible from the evidence’ and uncontradicted by other inferences or evidence, show that there is no triable issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” (Adler v. Manor Healthcare Corp. (1992) 7 Cal.App.4th 1110, 1119.)

 

As to each claim as framed by the complaint, the defendant moving for summary judgment must satisfy the initial burden of proof by presenting facts to negate an essential element, or to establish a defense. (CCP § 437c(p)(2).) Once the defendant has met that burden, “the burden shifts to the plaintiff to show that a triable issue of one or more material facts exists as to that cause of action or a defense thereto.” (Id.)  To establish a triable issue of material fact, the party opposing the motion must produce “substantial responsive evidence.” (Sangster v. Paetkau (1998) 68 Cal.App.4th 151, 166.) Courts “liberally construe the evidence in support of the party opposing summary judgment and resolve doubts concerning the evidence in favor of that party.” (Dore v. Arnold Worldwide, Inc. (2006) 39 Cal.4th 384, 389.)

 

Defendant Brenda Dietlein moves for summary judgment, or in the alternative, summary adjudication of Plaintiff’s claims. Defendant asserts that the complaint fails because there was no signed contract between the parties, Plaintiff is a “cancelled” entity, the claims are barred by the statute of limitations, and Plaintiff has committed misconduct.

 

A. Existence of Contract

 

Defendant asserts that the complaint fails because Plaintiff alleges that the parties had a written contract, but Plaintiff has admitted under oath that no contract exists. Defendant argues that this is a “fraud on the court” and that it bars the claim for breach of contract under the statute of frauds. In opposition, Plaintiff disputes that there is no written contract. Plaintiff represents that the parties did have a written contract, but Plaintiff has been unable to locate it. This is sufficient to create a triable issue of fact as to whether the parties had a written agreement. Summary judgment cannot be granted on this basis.

 

B. Standing

 

Defendant argues that Plaintiff cannot bring this action because “Farias Jett & Company” is a “cancelled” entity and thus does not have capacity to sue. In opposition, Plaintiff presents evidence showing that Plaintiff has maintained a proper fictitious business name through the filling of this action. Plaintiff also emphasizes that Plaintiff, as an individual, is the real party-in-interest. Summary judgment cannot be granted on this basis.

 

C. Statute of Limitations

 

Defendant asserts that all claims are barred by the two-year statute of limitations for oral contracts. Defendant argues that because the loans were issued in 2016-2017, Plaintiff had until 2018-2019 to file suit. In opposition, Plaintiff asserts that the action is ruled by the four-year statute of limitations for breach of written contract. Plaintiff also argues that even if the agreement was governed by a two-year statute, the action is timely. Plaintiff presents evidence showing that Plaintiff provided services to Defendant through September 2019 and that Defendant made the last payment on the loans in December 2019. Plaintiff filed this action in September 2021, less than two years after the last loan payment. This is sufficient to create a triable issue of fact as to the timeliness of the action.

 

D. Misconduct

 

Defendant argues that summary judgment must be granted because Plaintiff forged “hundreds” of checks using Defendant’s signature. Defendant argues that this shows Plaintiff has unclean hands and has tampered with evidence. In opposition, Plaintiff presents evidence showing he did not forge checks, but rather Defendant provided specific authorization for Plaintiff to use Defendant’s electronic signature on checks to the Glendale Centre Theatre. Summary judgment cannot be granted on this basis.

 

E. Nature of the Loans

 

Defendant asserts the complaint fails because Plaintiff has a documented history of predatory lending. Defendant also argues that the loans were not “loans” but instead were gifts and “barter arrangements.” In opposition, Plaintiff presents evidence showing Plaintiff made partial payments on the loan showing that she acknowledged that it was a loan and not a gift and showing that the parties’ arrangement was one involving cash, not a barter agreement for exchange of services. This is sufficient to create a triable issue of fact as to the nature of the loans.

 

F. Bill of Particulars

 

Defendant argues that the claim for account stated fails because Plaintiff failed to provide a “bill of particulars” to Defendant. In opposition, Plaintiff presents evidence showing that itemized bills were sent to Defendant. This is sufficient to create a triable issue of fact.

 

Defendant’s motion for summary judgment, or in the alternative, motion for summary adjudication is DENIED.
